input: The Nusselt number is a dimensionless quantity that is widely used in the study of convective heat transfer, and it can be understood as a comparison between two different mechanisms by which heat can be transferred at a surface. More specifically, the Nusselt number is defined as the ratio of convective heat transfer to conductive heat transfer at the surface in question. If the Nusselt number has a value near 1, this tells us that the two mechanisms are contributing roughly equally, and that the movement of the fluid is adding very little to the rate at which heat is transferred beyond what conduction through the fluid layer next to the surface would achieve on its own. On the other hand, if the Nusselt number is large, this indicates that convection is the dominant mechanism, and that the moving fluid is removing heat from the surface far more effectively than conduction alone would be able to do. The Nusselt number is therefore best thought of as a measure of how much the flow enhances the transfer of heat at the surface, expressed relative to the purely conductive case, which acts as the natural reference point for the comparison. It applies to the conditions actually prevailing at the surface, and it is in terms of those conditions that any particular value of the number has to be interpreted by the reader.
target: The Nusselt number compares two routes by which heat leaves a surface into a fluid: convection into the moving fluid, and conduction across the fluid layer that rests on the surface. The Nusselt number is defined as the ratio of convective to conductive heat transfer at the surface, and the conductive transfer is the reference against which the convective transfer is measured. A value near 1 means the two transfers are of the same size. Under that condition the moving fluid removes heat at about the rate at which conduction across the surface layer alone would remove it, and the motion of the fluid adds little to the transfer. A large value means convective transfer dominates the comparison: the moving fluid removes heat many times faster than conduction across the layer would, and the surface is held close to the temperature of the fluid by the flow. Both readings are taken at the surface and for the conditions at the surface, since the ratio compares the two mechanisms under one set of conditions rather than reporting a property of the fluid alone. The denominator of the ratio sets the floor of the scale. Conduction across the layer is the transfer that would remain if the fluid were still, so the number states how far the actual transfer stands above that floor for the same surface and the same driving temperature difference. Read in this way, the number ranks a surface condition by the standing of convection against its own reference, and the ranking is the whole content of the value.
